I love Void Stranger, but I understand it won't be for everyone. The main gameplay mechanic in this game is akin to sliding block puzzles, where you are given tiles you can move and have to navigate from A to B. There are some sections (mainly later in the game) that require intense headscratching, maybe head-bashing-into-the-wall too. If you're struggling and can't find it in yourself to enjoy this sort of thing, there's a good guide made by a steam user Brilli for the later section of the game I used occasionally. You'll know the part I'm talking about when the game suddenly becomes much, much more difficult. Even though it's good to discover everything yourself, it's just not fun to be stuck on the same one room for up to twenty minutes or more sometimes, or maybe that's just me.

I would very highly recommend discovering absolutely everything yourself. There is a certain category that Void Stranger falls into, one that games very rarely fall into, a category of game I've always wanted to create myself but never have had quite enough grit to finish one. What I mean is a kind of game that spells nothing out to you - you'll never find a tutorial in this sort of game, no item descriptions, no in-game item cataloguing everything you encounter. If you used the wiki in the Binding of Isaac, if you looked up the map in Rain World, if you quit ANIMAL WELL or FEZ or TUNIC because they were too confusing, then maybe this isn't for you. I don't know, I just find these kinds of games incredibly rewarding when you discover something new by yourself.

When I first played Void Stranger, maybe 10 hours in, I thought I was completely finished. I had reached the first ending and was content with the game, and dropped it. A few days later I was thinking about a loose end I hadn't yet cut, and reopened the game to check it out. It turned out that loose end was the first step that led me down a rabbit hole, and now I'm 50 hours in and still not even halfway finished. Void stranger just keeps on giving; it is as large as you let it be, and not in the same "replayability" way that some roguelikes are, for example (not that those games are in any way worse for that).

A unique game that tests your perseverance, and asks you to continually question and experiment with everything. The puzzles of the game go beyond any individual level, and instead ask you to break open the puzzle of the void itself. A wonderful mind-bending adventure that requires you learn and become a part of it's world.

The game doesn't really respect your time as a player is the short and sweet of it. A lack of undo button and ways to easily navigate to previous levels means you're spending hours fixing a mistake you made by accidentally going down a set of stairs. This is alleviated later on somewhat but it's very much too little too late.

The meta puzzles are also oddly bland, being the same thing over and over. Even one of the cooler bits of meta mechanics ends up being mostly a way to refresh your life count. 

I did enjoy the storytelling of the game though and would consider that it's strongest aspect. 

Lastly, the ending of the game is just plain bizarre in terms of gameplay. The last hour I spent with this game was just not at all fun and threw away all the cool puzzles leading up to it in the route.

The game is just outshined by a decent amount of other puzzle games in the genre and the hype seems a little odd to me.

Void Stranger really is quite a strange game. On the surface it is just a slow and grindy sokoban puzzler, but there’s lots of gameplay secrets and a ton of narrative and worldbuilding hidden deep within. Going through floor after floor of puzzles can feel quite tedious, especially since you may have to replay some of the same puzzles many times. Most of the game’s secrets are clever and satisfying to discover, but some are very obscure and strange, and some make the game much more difficult if you don’t discover them in a timely fashion.
It uses its pixel graphics and limited color palette well to create a modern yet nostalgic visual style and the soundtrack is also uncommonly good. It’s a very genuine and touching piece of art but the potential frustrating slowness of the puzzle grind might kill a lot of players’ motivation before they can experience it. However I can’t see it as anything but the creators’ pure intentions for it to be designed this way, and as a game developed by a very small team it’s an incredible achievement.
Very good game, well made! Would strongly recommend to puzzle folks.

To keep this as vague as I can while still pointing out how awesome this title is, the core gameplay loop is a twist on the old block puzzle games a la Sokoban or The Adventures of LoLo, right down to being thoroughly engrossing.  It draws you in through immersive gameplay and is immensely absorbing and immersive.

In many other ways this game reminds me of celeste.  The game is very difficult in a good way, has AMAZING music, and has a much more interesting and deep story and narrative then you might think for this sort of title.

The hardest part about writing this review is I want to gush about the game, but the fact that this is game best experienced without knowing anything beforehand makes that tough.

Suffice to say you should go buy and play it.

This is a cautious thumbs up.

First, what I liked about this game: lots of secrets.  What I did not like about this game: all the damn backtracking.  It's actually really satisfying to play through, but finding the secrets is painful, and I gave up after reaching the True Ending without bothering with any post-game content because, honestly, I'm done.  I've spent long enough on this.  It was fun for a long time, but then it wasn't.

So, what's backtracking?  This is sometimes controversial.  See, I really enjoy MV games, where you revisit the same places multiple times.  La-Mulana, my favorite game of all time, involved probably a hundred hours of doing this.  La-Mulana 2, that one was actually 100 hours of playtime on my blind playthrough.  But in those games, you can travel anywhere you want pretty much instantly.  Sure, not every room is easily accessible, but there are generally pretty good warp points to get to wherever you want to be easily.  Void Stranger, on the other hand...  Basically, you need to replay the whole game if you want to try something again.  Sure, there are some shortcuts and a couple of ways to make this easier, but in general, you're just out of luck.  That's just plain frustrating.  And I get it, thematically, but it's not fun.  Subsequent runs of the game are easier but they're still annoying.  This morning, I went to the kitchen to make lunch.  This evening, I went to the kitchen again to make dinner.  I would not call that backtracking; I would call that revisiting the room.  La-Mulana has revisiting.  But Void Stranger, with its frustrating replay of the game, has backtracking.

Anyway, I did enjoy this game for many hours, and I think the main bit of the game is legitimately enjoyable.  At some point, though, it's worth it to just use a guide, because the secrets stop being fun to discover on your own, in my opinion.

Also, there's a lot of... the female form.  A *lot* of it.  It's a little weird?  I have to hope my wife or my kids don't come in during those scenes.  It's not explicit, exactly, but... yeah.

Great music, though!
